parts.partTitle: Why Java Needs 6 Lines for Hello World

beats.headline: Why does Java need 6 lines for Hello World?
beats.subline: It isn't random boilerplate. Every single keyword is solving a real engineering problem.
beats.narration: Python prints Hello World in one line. Java takes six. If you think that's just bloated ceremony, let's decode what every single line actually tells the compiler and the JVM.

beats.title: Scripting vs. Enterprise Blueprint

bottom.label: Standard Java
points: Prevents naming clashes across big teams
Catches type & structure bugs at compile time

beats.narration: In standard Java, statements can't float loosely at the top of a file. Statements live inside methods, methods live inside a class, and classes live inside packages.

beats.title: Packages, Imports & Class Rules

steps.explanation: Maps directly to folders on disk (com/javahub/basics/) and stops class name collisions like two different Order classes.
Compile-time shorthand only—unlike C's #include, it never copies code. Bonus: java.lang is auto-imported for you.
Filename MUST match the public class name—exact capitalization: HelloWorld.java.

beats.narration: First, package mirrors your folders on disk so two Order classes never collide. Next, import is just compile-time shorthand with zero runtime cost, and java dot lang is imported automatically. Then public class HelloWorld must match your filename letter for letter.

beats.title: Decoding public static void main

steps.explanation: At startup, zero objects exist yet. Marking main static lets the JVM call HelloWorld.main(args) directly—and args is never null, just empty.
System (java.lang class) → out (static PrintStream field) → println() (instance method that prints + newline).

beats.narration: Why is main static? Because at startup, no object exists yet, so the JVM calls main directly on the class, passing command-line flags in args, which is never null. Inside, System is a class, out is a static PrintStream field, and println prints your line.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: static main = JVM entry with no object

beats.narration: That's the blueprint. In Part 2, we crack open HelloWorld dot class with javap to see the exact bytecode the JVM executes.

parts.partTitle: What Happens When You Run javac & java?

beats.headline: Your CPU cannot read Java.
beats.subline: Here is the exact 2-phase pipeline turning .java into native machine speed.
beats.narration: Your CPU has no idea what Java source code is. Every time you build and run a Java app, your code passes through a strict two-phase pipeline.

beats.title: From Source to Native CPU
beats.subtitle: Compile once with javac → run anywhere on the JVM

nodes.label: Class Loader & Verifier
nodes.detail: Checks stack bounds, types & access rules before running

nodes.label: Execution Engine (JIT + GC)
nodes.detail: Interprets & JIT-compiles hot paths into native CPU instructions

beats.narration: Phase one: javac compiles your dot java file into portable dot class bytecode. Phase two: the JVM loads it, runs the Bytecode Verifier to guarantee memory and type safety, and then the Execution Engine JIT-compiles hot code straight into native CPU instructions.

beats.title: Compiling & Running Packages
beats.caption: Avoid the #1 classpath mistake!

lines.text: # 1. Compile and mirror package folders into out/

beats.narration: When using packages from the terminal, pass dash d out to javac so it mirrors your folder tree. Then run java with dash cp pointing to the root folder out, followed by the dotted class name—never slashes, and never dot class.

beats.title: Disassembling with javap -c -p
beats.caption: Two hidden things javac generated for you
beats.narration: Run javap dash c dash p on that class file and two cool things jump out. First, javac silently synthesized a default constructor calling Object. Second, main is literally three instructions: getstatic System dot out, load the string constant, and invokevirtual println.

beats.title: Now You See Inside .class
takeaways: javac → portable bytecode; JVM → native speed

beats.narration: Now you know what's actually inside a dot class file. In Part 3, see the one-character semicolon bug that silently breaks if-checks, plus Java 25's brand new 3-line main.

parts.partTitle: Silent Semicolon Bug, Javadoc & Java 25 Compact Main

beats.headline: One stray semicolon can bypass your auth check.
beats.subline: It compiles with zero errors—and runs your protected block every single time.
beats.narration: Java doesn't care about indentation—it trusts semicolons and curly braces. Which means one tiny stray semicolon can compile cleanly and completely wreck your logic.

beats.title: The Empty-Statement Semicolon Trap

top.label: Compiles, Always Runs!

bottom.label: Clean Block Scope
points: No semicolon after if / for / while headers

beats.narration: Look at that semicolon right after if isAuthorized. In Java, a lone semicolon is a valid empty statement, so the if ends immediately and the sensitive block below runs every single time. Never put a semicolon after an if or loop header.

beats.title: Comments & Javadoc (Zero Bytecode Cost)

steps.explanation: Stripped completely by javac—zero bytes in .class! Use them to document non-obvious business rules.
Starts with TWO asterisks. IDEs render @param, @return & @throws on hover, and javadoc generates HTML docs.

beats.narration: Comments never even make it into bytecode. Use double-slash to explain why, not what. And for public APIs, use Javadoc starting with slash-star-star—your IDE renders param, return, and throws right on hover.

beats.title: Modern Java: Compact Source Files

top.label: Production Standard (Java 8–25+)

bottom.label: Java 25 (JEP 512 Finalized)
points: Compiler still wraps it in a class under the hood

beats.narration: Finally, modern Java heard the complaints. After previews starting in Java 21, Java 25 finalized JEP 512: just void main and IO dot println. Under the hood the compiler still wraps it in a class, so you still need standard syntax for real production services.

takeaways: No stray semicolons after if / for headers
Javadoc (/**) powers IDE hover & HTML docs
Java 25 JEP 512 gives a 3-line main() on-ramp
